newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Auspine sees half year loss A$6.3 mln.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Auspine sees half year loss A$6.3 mln.

text.p: Timber products group Auspine Ltd said on Friday it expects to post an after tax operating loss of A$6.3 million for the first half of 1996/97, including abnormal charges of about A$15 million.

However Chairman Geoff Hill told the company's annual meeting that with no worsening market conditions directors expected to turn the business around and achieve a small profit within the fourth quarter of 1996/97.
Auspine said on October 23 that it expected net loss before abnormals of A$5 million in the first half.
"Currently we expect the half year result to be in the vicinity of a A$7.3 million operating loss before tax (A$6.3 million after tax)," Hill said on Friday.
Abnormals for the half-year included inventory writedowns of A$5 million, a A$6.5 million restructure provision, and A$3.5 million contingencies, he said.
"These non-recurring writedowns and provisions represent a clearing of the decks at Auspine to ensure the company is in good shape for what we see as a bright and positive future," he said.
Hill said market forces had been unkind to Auspine and its competitors due to a significant and harsher than expected downturn in the building cycle and intense competition.
Auspine reported a massive slump in its net profit for 1995/96 to A$4.45 million from A$17.25 million a year earlier.

Hill said key initiatives of a new business plan to be put in place over the next few months included a business-wide management strategy, focus on improving net returns, downsizing of non-core operations and an ongoing cost reduction programme.

"As a result of the steps taken at the half-year mark and the initiatives put in place for the balance of the year, your directors expect, subject to there being no worsening in the competitive position, to turn the business around and achieve a small profit within the fourth quarter of 1996/97," he said.
Hill recently replaced former chairman Rod Hartley, who resigned in September after a public dispute with managing director and major shareholder Adrian de Bruin.
The new chairman said the company was vulnerable to takeover given the strategic nature of its assets.

"However predators should be aware that control of this company resides around the board talbe and it will be Austpine's board of directors and shareholders who will decide on any change in control," Hill said.
